bio-001.why: Statins occupy the substrate-binding site of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA (HMG-CoA) reductase. By competing with HMG-CoA, they reduce mevalonate production and slow cholesterol synthesis in the liver.

notes.B: AMP-activated protein kinase can phosphorylate and inhibit the reductase when cellular energy is scarce.
notes.C: An upstream kinase activates AMP-activated protein kinase, placing it a step removed from the enzyme that binds statins.
notes.D: The phosphatase removes an inhibitory phosphate from the reductase, restoring its activity independently of statin binding.
notes.E: Protein kinase A transmits signals from cyclic AMP, whereas statins bind the enzyme that produces mevalonate.

bio-002.why: When cellular energy is scarce, AMP-activated protein kinase phosphorylates HMG-CoA reductase. This reduces the production of mevalonate and slows the energy-consuming synthesis of cholesterol.

notes.A: The reductase converts HMG-CoA into mevalonate and receives its inhibitory phosphate from a separate kinase.
notes.C: An upstream kinase activates AMP-activated protein kinase, which then directly phosphorylates the reductase.
notes.D: The phosphatase removes the inhibitory phosphate from HMG-CoA reductase, allowing cholesterol synthesis to resume.
notes.E: Protein kinase A responds to cyclic AMP, whereas the enzyme that directly senses energy status and inhibits the reductase is AMP-activated protein kinase.

bio-003.why: An upstream kinase phosphorylates a threonine in the catalytic subunit of AMP-activated protein kinase. This phosphorylation allows the energy sensor to inhibit biosynthetic pathways when energy is scarce.

notes.A: HMG-CoA reductase makes mevalonate and is a downstream target of the activated energy sensor.
notes.B: AMP-activated protein kinase is the enzyme receiving the activating phosphate in this signalling step.
notes.D: The reductase phosphatase restores the activity of the cholesterol-synthesis enzyme by removing its inhibitory phosphate.
notes.E: Protein kinase A responds to cyclic AMP, whereas a distinct upstream kinase phosphorylates the activation loop of the energy sensor.

bio-004.why: Cyclic AMP binds the regulatory subunits of protein kinase A and releases its active catalytic subunits. This is how the hormonal signal is relayed to downstream enzymes regulating cholesterol synthesis.

notes.A: HMG-CoA reductase makes mevalonate and is the enzyme whose activity changes downstream of the hormonal signal.
notes.B: AMP-activated protein kinase can phosphorylate the reductase directly, but its regulatory nucleotide is AMP rather than cyclic AMP.
notes.C: An upstream kinase phosphorylates AMP-activated protein kinase and does not serve as the receptor for cyclic AMP in this pathway.
notes.D: The reductase phosphatase activates the reductase by removing phosphate and acts downstream of the cyclic AMP signal.

bio-005.why: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase uses ATP, bicarbonate and the cofactor biotin to convert acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA. This commits carbon to fatty acid synthesis and controls the supply of two-carbon units for elongation.

notes.A: Condensation takes place on fatty acid synthase once the carboxylase has supplied the malonyl group.
notes.B: Acetate can be activated to acetyl-CoA, but this also supplies pathways other than fatty acid synthesis.
notes.C: The carboxylase adds bicarbonate-derived carbon to acetyl-CoA, so free malonate is not its starting material.
notes.E: The first reduction on fatty acid synthase consumes NADPH after the chain has already undergone condensation.

bio-006.why: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, glucose can supply acetyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis and glycerol 3-phosphate for the backbone. Insulin favours esterification of the fatty acids into triacylglycerol for storage.

notes.A: Plants also synthesise triacylglycerols, which are an important energy reserve in many seeds.
notes.C: Low carbohydrate availability generally favours oxidation of fatty acids and reduces the use of carbohydrate carbon for new fatty acids.
notes.D: Animals synthesise triacylglycerols in the fed state, including in the liver and adipose tissue.
notes.E: A sustained carbohydrate surplus supplies both carbon and an insulin signal for fat storage in humans.

bio-007.why: Insulin favours storage after a carbohydrate-rich meal. Glucose supplies glycerol 3-phosphate for the triacylglycerol backbone and can supply acetyl-CoA for synthesis of the attached fatty acids.

notes.A: Fat is stored with little water and yields more energy per gram than hydrated glycogen.
notes.C: Insulin promotes fatty acid synthesis and storage after feeding, while low insulin favours release of fatty acids from adipose tissue.
notes.D: Mammalian liver can convert surplus glucose into fatty acids and esterify these to form triacylglycerols.
notes.E: Phosphatidate loses its phosphate to form diacylglycerol, which receives a third fatty acyl group.

bio-008.why: In the cytidine diphosphate (CDP) routes, one partner is activated and the other supplies a free hydroxyl group. Linking two CDP-activated partners is unnecessary for forming the phosphodiester bond.

notes.A: CDP-choline transfers its phosphocholine group to diacylglycerol during the formation of phosphatidylcholine.
notes.B: Free inositol reacts with activated CDP-diacylglycerol in the pathway that forms phosphatidylinositol.
notes.D: Mammalian cells can exchange serine for the ethanolamine head group of phosphatidylethanolamine to make phosphatidylserine.
notes.E: The liver can synthesise phosphatidylcholine by adding three methyl groups to the head group of phosphatidylethanolamine.

bio-009.why: Low-density lipoprotein carries much of the cholesterol in plasma as cholesteryl esters. Cells can bind its apolipoprotein B-100 through LDL receptors and take up the particle by endocytosis.

notes.A: Intermediate-density lipoprotein is a remnant that can return to the liver or give rise to low-density lipoprotein.
notes.C: High-density lipoprotein accepts excess cholesterol from peripheral cells and participates in its return to the liver.
notes.D: Chylomicrons chiefly deliver dietary triacylglycerol, and their cholesterol-rich remnants are taken up by the liver.
notes.E: Very-low-density lipoprotein chiefly exports hepatic triacylglycerol and gives rise to cholesterol-enriched particles as it loses fat.

bio-010.why: The liver packages triacylglycerol into very-low-density lipoprotein for export. Lipoprotein lipase then hydrolyses the particle's triacylglycerol in capillaries, making fatty acids available to muscle and adipose tissue.

notes.A: Chylomicrons are rich in triacylglycerol too, but the intestine produces them to transport fat absorbed from a meal.
notes.B: Low-density lipoprotein has already lost much of its precursor's triacylglycerol and is enriched in cholesteryl esters.
notes.D: High-density lipoprotein participates mainly in cholesterol transport and carries a relatively small amount of triacylglycerol.
notes.E: Intermediate-density lipoprotein is the remnant formed after lipoprotein lipase has removed some triacylglycerol from the hepatic particle.

bio-011.why: Acetyl-CoA supplies all the carbon atoms retained in cholesterol. Its two-carbon units first form acetoacetyl-CoA and then HMG-CoA, which is reduced to mevalonate in the sterol pathway.

notes.A: Free acetate must first be activated with coenzyme A before it can enter cholesterol synthesis.
notes.C: Oxaloacetate can help export acetyl units as citrate, but is regenerated when cytosolic citrate is cleaved.
notes.D: Malate participates in the citrate shuttle and can help supply reducing power for biosynthesis.
notes.E: Pyruvate can yield acetyl-CoA through oxidative decarboxylation, placing it upstream of the direct building block.

bio-012.why: Cholecystokinin is a peptide hormone synthesised from an amino acid precursor in intestinal endocrine cells. The other choices are sterols or products of sterol metabolism.

notes.A: The liver oxidises and shortens the side chain of cholesterol to form primary bile acids, including chenodeoxycholic acid.
notes.B: Glycocholic acid forms when the liver conjugates the cholesterol-derived bile acid cholic acid with glycine.
notes.C: Steroid-producing cells convert cholesterol to pregnenolone, from which they can synthesise testosterone.
notes.D: In skin, ultraviolet B light acts on the sterol precursor 7-dehydrocholesterol to initiate vitamin D₃ synthesis.
